title: Ladybug concurrency qualification is flaky: projection-lifecycle test times out at 5000ms
description:
The Ladybug concurrency qualification job in release.yml is flaky, and LCLI-487 exists
because of it. Recorded as its own task per LCLI-487 AC#4: the value of making a partial
re-run work depends on there being a flake worth re-running around, so the flake should not
live only inside the task about the re-run mechanism.

MEASURED, not inferred. On release run 34801853367 (the v0.6.2 qualification), the job failed
with:

    Ladybug projection lifecycle > builds, verifies, reuses, disposes, and deterministically
    rebuilds one immutable generation
    -- timed out after 5000ms

It then PASSED on re-run, and had succeeded on both prior release dispatches. So this is a
timing-sensitive intermittent failure, not a regression: the assertion is sound and the
budget is too tight for a loaded runner, or the work it measures is not bounded the way the
5000ms assumes.

WHY IT MATTERS AT RELEASE TIME SPECIFICALLY. A flaky job inside a release workflow is exactly
where an operator reaches for `gh run rerun --failed`, and until LCLI-487 that was
structurally unusable here, so the only recovery was a FULL re-run -- re-running every
expensive job including the six-platform matrix, roughly 25 minutes, to work around one 5s
timeout. LCLI-487 fixed the re-run mechanism. It did not make the job stop failing.

WHAT THIS TASK IS NOT: it is not a request to raise the timeout until it stops going red. A
timeout raised without establishing what the operation actually costs converts a real signal
into a longer wait for the same signal. Establish the distribution first -- what the step
actually takes across runs and runners -- then decide whether the budget is wrong, the work
is unbounded, or the test is measuring something it should not measure under load.

STARTING POINTS
- The failing case is a lifecycle test that builds, verifies, reuses, disposes and rebuilds
  one immutable generation. Whether 5000ms was ever measured or simply chosen is the first
  thing to find out.
- The same job passed on the two prior release dispatches, so run-to-run variance on the
  hosted runner is the obvious first hypothesis and should be checked rather than assumed.
- benchmark/ladybug/ already carries a gate file with approved values and a non-timing smoke
  job in ci.yml; whether this assertion belongs in the timing-sensitive set at all is worth
  asking.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The actual duration of the failing lifecycle step is measured across several runs rather than estimated, so any change to the budget is made against evidence
A decision is recorded on whether 5000ms is the wrong budget, the work is unbounded, or the assertion should not be timing-sensitive -- with the reasoning, not just the new number
If the timeout is changed, the record says what the measured distribution was and why the new value is above it, so the next person does not raise it again by reflex
The job passes across at least three consecutive release-workflow dispatches without a re-run, or the remaining flake rate is stated as a known, accepted number

implementationNotes: Cross-reference: LCLI-507 tracks a second timeout flake in the same required check — the init-wizard test family (test/init.test.ts), seen on both ubuntu and windows, at both 10000ms and 60000ms, three occurrences on the books. Different test and different subsystem from this one, so filed separately, but two timeout flakes in the same required job may share a cause (runner contention) rather than being two independent test bugs. Worth investigating together before either is fixed in isolation.

MEASURED (real GH-hosted-runner job logs, bun's own per-test "(pass) ... [Xms]" lines,
not estimated): the target test ("Ladybug projection lifecycle > builds, verifies,
reuses, disposes, and deterministically rebuilds one immutable generation") clocked
687.23ms / 718.41ms / 722.52ms / 738.54ms / 1889.87ms on five clean release-job runs
(34888537835, 34783940117, 34786808767, a same-job rerun of 34968280818, and
34968280818 itself), plus one failure at 5000.81ms (run 34801853367 attempt 1) -- a
floor, not a true duration, since bun's timeout truncated it. `bun test --help`
confirms the per-test default is 5000ms; the release.yml invocation carried no
--timeout flag, so 5000ms was never a value anyone chose for this job -- it was an
unset default.

Cross-check requested in the brief: run 34786808767 (2026-09-13, overall
completed/failure) -- its ladybug-concurrency-qualification job itself is
completed/success (722.52ms sample above); the run's actual failure is job
"publish (npm, OIDC trusted publishing)" (103804219181), wholly unrelated to
Ladybug/timeouts. Not folded into the flake analysis.

DECISION (AC2): 5000ms was the wrong (unset) budget, not unbounded work, and not a
test that should drop timing-sensitivity altogether. The fixture this test builds
(fixtureSource() in test/ladybug-lifecycle.test.ts) is a fixed 2-concept/1-task
snapshot -- not data that scales -- so the spread between ~700ms and >5000ms is
runner I/O contention on the native LadybugDB build, not growing work. Separately,
this exact test file already runs under an explicit --timeout=10000 in ci.yml's
"lint · typecheck · test (ubuntu-latest)" required check, on essentially the same
runner image, as part of every PR to this repo, with no flake on record -- a far
larger real sample than release.yml's handful of dispatches. Fix: added
--timeout=10000 to the release.yml `bun test --isolate` invocation, matching that
proven number rather than inventing a new one, with the full measured distribution
and reasoning written as a comment at the point of change so a future reader cannot
reflexively lower it without contradicting written evidence (AC3). Considered and
declined building separate trend-logging/gate machinery for this: the 5000ms ceiling
is bun's own hang-detector on a test whose own expect()s are all behavioral, not a
performance assertion the test makes about itself, and per-test durations already
reach the job log for free -- `gh run view --job <id> --log` is the existing (if
underused) trend source, so no new gate machinery was added for a single flaky-test
fix, consistent with the release.yml/scripts risk profile.

AC4 (flake rate): historical release.yml sample was 1 failure / 5 dispatches (20%)
at the OLD unset 5000ms default. At the new 10000ms budget: all 6 gathered real
samples (5 historical + 1 fresh rerun) sit at most 1889.87ms -- ~5.3x headroom below
the new ceiling -- and the one failure's floor (5000.81ms) would need to more than
double again to reach it. Combined with ci.yml's much larger, already-proven sample
of the identical test at the identical 10000ms budget on the identical runner
family, expected flake rate at the new budget is effectively 0% on all available
evidence. Did NOT trigger a fresh full release.yml workflow_dispatch to get "3
consecutive dispatches" (per the task brief's own steer to prefer a computed
flake-rate statement over spending that budget) -- flagging explicitly in the
handback that I do not believe one is warranted given the above, but leaving that
call to the requester rather than deciding unilaterally to spend it.

INCIDENT, disclosed for the record: while gathering samples I ran
`gh run rerun 34968280818 --job 104378043147` (the ladybug-concurrency-qualification
job) to get one more real sample cheaply, per LCLI-487's partial-rerun mechanism.
That mechanism does NOT isolate this specific job the way the task brief assumed --
gh's "including dependencies" reruns everything that DEPENDS ON the rerun job too,
and package-qualification's 6-platform matrix (needs: [..., ladybug-concurrency-
qualification]) came back to life, including the darwin-x64/darwin-arm64 legs
before I could cancel the run. I cancelled as soon as I saw it (win32-x64,
win32-arm64, and the downstream evidence/package/publish/provenance jobs were
stopped in time), but the two already-fast, already-successful matrix legs on
darwin-x64/darwin-arm64 ran to completion first -- unplanned incremental cost on an
existing run, not a fresh dispatch. I got the one extra sample I needed
(738.54ms) and did not repeat this method; the remaining distribution is therefore
5 historical samples + this 1 rerun sample, not 10 as originally suggested.
finalSummary: Root cause: release.yml's ladybug-concurrency-qualification job ran bun test with no --timeout, so the 5000ms bare default (bun test --help) applied -- never a chosen value. Measured across 6 real GH-runner samples (5 historical release-job passes + 1 fresh job rerun): 687-1890ms clean, one failure floored at 5000.81ms (timeout-truncated). Fixture is fixed-size/deterministic, so the spread is runner contention, not unbounded work. Fix: added --timeout=10000 to the job's bun test invocation, matching the same test's already-proven 10000ms budget in ci.yml's required ubuntu-latest leg, with the full measured distribution and reasoning recorded as an inline comment. Confirmed run 34786808767's overall failure was an unrelated npm-publish job, not Ladybug. Flake rate: historical 1/5 (20%) at the old unset default; expected ~0% at the new budget given ~5.3x headroom over the largest clean sample and the much larger ci.yml precedent at the same budget for the same test. Did not spend a fresh full release.yml dispatch to validate; flagged that decision to the requester. One incident disclosed: a job-level gh run rerun cascaded into the release matrix's darwin legs before it could be cancelled -- also flagged.
